context_messages.content: Hello! I am Xiao. It is afternoon. I have a break now.
Hello, Xiao! I am Lin. Yes, it is warm in Tianhe today. I am drinking coffee.
Me too! The coffee is good. I like the American style cups.
Oh, well, we like Chinese tea more here. By the way, do you want some roasted tea leaves?
Maybe later. I am working on my computer now. It is very fast.
That is good. My computer is a bit slow. Do you play table tennis at the park?
Yes! I play every weekend. The court is near my home.
Wow, table tennis is fun! I see many people play there. Do you have a racket?
Yes, I have one. It is red and black. I like the color.
Red and black is nice! Well, I should go back to work soon. See you later?
Yes, see you. I will go home for lunch soon.
Good idea. What do you eat for lunch? I usually eat dumplings.
Dumplings are great! I eat them too. They are hot and tasty.

context_messages.content: Hello. I am Chen Hong. My head hurts.
Hello, Chen Hong. I'm Nurse nurse Li. Please sit down here.
Thank you. Can I drink some warm tea?
Yes, of course. It is very good for your head.
I think the new law about traffic in Hangzhou is very bad.
Well, I understand. But now, let's focus on your health. Do you want to rest in bed for ten minutes?
Yes, please. I need to rest.
Good. The bed is soft and warm. It helps you relax.
My family is far away in Beijing. I miss them.
Oh, that is sad. But it's winter now, and you should eat hot food like wontons.
Wontons are my favorite food. I like them very much.
That is great! Wontons are delicious. We can order them later when you are better.
How much time do I need to rest?
You can rest for twenty minutes. Then, we will check your temperature again.
Thank you, nurse Li. You are very kind.

Hello, Chen Hong. I am Nurse nurse Li. Please sit down here. It is cold today.
Yes. The room is cold. I need to drink some hot water.
That is good. I will give you warm ginger tea. It helps with the head.
Thank you. People in my family believe in gods for health.
Well, that is nice. By the way, do you like eating hot pot?
Yes, I like it very much. Do you have a hot pot at home?
No, I am busy. My family usually eats noodles at home.
Okay. My grandma makes very good soup noodles.
That sounds delicious. I want to try your grandma's noodles.
You should visit her next time. She lives in Hangzhou.
Yes, Hangzhou is a nice city. It has many beautiful lakes.
I want to rest in bed now. The tea is warm.

context_messages.content: Hello, I am Li Na. I am in Hangzhou. It is hot today. My family and I take a taxi.
Hello, Li Na! Yes, it is very hot in Hangzhou now. I am Driver Wang. Where do you want to go?
We want to go to West Lake. Do you know the way? It is nice there.
Yes, I know West Lake very well. It is beautiful. We go there in ten minutes. I drive slowly.
Okay. I drink water. I do not like alcohol or dating with strangers.
Well, drinking water is good in this heat! You are right, Li Na. We should not meet strangers for drinks. It is not safe. Anyway, I will take you to the park. It is very quiet there.
Yes, I like quiet places. My son plays there. He likes to see the boats.
That sounds fun! Your son is lucky. The boats on the lake are small and red. They look like ducks. My grandson also goes there.
Oh yes. How much do we pay for the taxi? Can I use my phone?
Of course! You can pay with your phone. You scan the QR code. It is very easy. Do you have Alipay?
Yes, I do. I have Alipay. I want to buy some fruit after we arrive.
Good idea! There is a market near the lake. You can buy fresh lychees and watermelons. They are sweet and cold.
I love watermelons. My husband eats it every day. What time is it now?
It is three o'clock. The sun is still high. We are almost at the gate. You can see the big willow trees.
Yes, I see them. They are tall and green. Thank you, Mr. Wang. You are a good driver.

I have a high fever. My head hurts a lot.
Oh, I see. Let me check your temperature. It is very hot.
Yes. Also, my family believes in Taoism. It is very important for me.
Well, thank you for telling me. By the way, are you drinking enough water today? It is very cold in Harbin.
No, I only drink tea. I want to buy some medicine now.
I can help you. We have fever medicine in the clinic. Do you want to take it now?
Yes please. How much does it cost? I have only some money.
It is twenty yuan. It is not expensive. Here is the medicine. Please take two pills.
Thank you doctor. I will go home and rest on my bed.
That is good. You should eat some hot porridge. It is warm and good for your stomach.
I will eat porridge. Do I need to see a specialist later?
No, rest at home for two days. If you are still sick, then come back to Nangang clinic.
Okay. I will call my daughter tomorrow. She lives in Harbin.

No, no headache. But my throat hurts a lot.
I understand. You can buy some medicine from the pharmacy nearby. What is your name again?
My name is Fang. I will buy some medicine. Do you have any cough syrup?

Thank you doctor. Will I need to take a taxi to go home?
Yes, the snow is very heavy. You can take a taxi. I will write the address for you.
Okay. I will stay at home and rest. I like hot food when I am sick.
That is good. You can eat some porridge or soup. It is very warm for your stomach.
Great. Thank you for your help. I feel a little better now.

Yes, that is fine. Can I pay by WeChat?

That sounds fun. But I heard some people drink too much alcohol when they go out to find friends.

I love Chinese calligraphy. Can I learn how to write my name in calligraphy style?
Of course! It is very traditional and beautiful. I will show you how to hold the brush properly first.
Thanks. Will we eat lunch together after the activity? I am a bit hungry now.
Yes, we can go to a nearby noodle shop. My favorite dish is beef noodle soup with hot oil. It tastes very good.
Beef noodle soup sounds delicious. Can I also bring some friends from my class to join us?
That is a wonderful idea! I think they will like the calligraphy too. Just tell them to arrive at ten o'clock sharp.
I will tell them now. Thank you very much for helping me join the group.

Yes, of course. I will take a long walk near the lake.
That sounds perfect. See you next time, Li Hua.

context_messages.content: Hello! I'm Li. I'm looking for a gift for my students' parents. They live in Donghu, Wuhan.
Hi Li! That's very kind of you. Actually, there are many good local brands here. For example, you can buy nice tea or silk scarves from the market near Huanghelou.
Yes, I like those things. But sometimes I worry about bad news in the world. I feel like violence is everywhere now.

I understand you might feel worried sometimes. However, let's talk about something happier. Have you tried the new electric kettles from local brands? They are very useful for making tea in your home.
Oh, really? Where can I see them?
Well, you can go to the supermarket in Xueyuan Road. It is not far from the subway station. They sell many small electronic products there.
Is it open on Wednesday evening? I want to go with my friend.
Yes, it is open until 9 pm. In addition, the air in Donghu is quite fresh in the spring. It is a good time to walk after shopping.
That sounds nice. Do you think the delivery is fast?
To be honest, delivery is very fast in Wuhan. If you buy online, it usually arrives tomorrow. But buying here lets you check the quality first.
I see. Maybe I will buy a set of tea cups for my neighbor's birthday next week.
That is a great idea! You know, handmade cups are popular now. They are cheaper than imported ones and very pretty.
Okay, I will ask my friend to help me choose one.

Hello Li! Yes, we have many good choices here. For example, local brands like Xiaomi or Huawei make great smartphones that work well with our mobile payment system. Also, smart home devices are very popular in the Donghu area now.
That sounds nice. Actually, I've been feeling really stressed lately because of work, and sometimes I feel like things are just too much to handle.

Oh, I can hear that you're feeling very overwhelmed right now. It's important to talk to a trusted friend or family member about how you feel, maybe someone you can call for support. By the way, have you thought about buying a nice box of hot pot ingredients for your students' parents? That is a traditional and warm gift in Wuhan.
Yes, talking to my friend helps a lot. Do you have any specific hot pot sets that deliver quickly?

Well, we have a special set from the local market near Hankou. It comes with all the sauces and fresh vegetables you need. Delivery is usually very fast here, especially in the evening. Have you used delivery services from this mall before?
Yes, I've used them since I moved to Wuhan. The speed is usually good, but sometimes the packaging gets wet.

That's true, rain can be a problem in spring sometimes. However, if you order from us, we use waterproof boxes for food orders. In addition, many people in Jiangxi province also prefer this style of packaging. Would you like to see the different soup bases we have?
Sure, please show me the spicy one. Is it too hot for older people?

Good question. We have a mild spicy base that is perfect for elders, though it still tastes very delicious. For example, many families in Changsha buy this specific type for their relatives. Also, you could add some fresh duck blood slices which are very common here.
I think that would be a great idea. Do you think I should add some drinks too?

Yes, I think you should! We have excellent Chinese tea that goes very well with hot pot. For instance, a pot of Osmanthus tea is a nice touch for a family gathering. To be honest, it makes the whole gift much more thoughtful.
Perfect. Let's get that set then. How much will it cost with delivery?

The set with the mild spice base and the tea will be around three hundred yuan, and delivery to your address will be included. That's a very reasonable price for such a high-quality gift. Would you like to pay with WeChat or Alipay?
WeChat is fine. Thanks for your help, Shop Assistant.

context_messages.content: Hi, I'm Hua. I just moved to an apartment in Min'an, Xiamen, and I'm feeling a bit overwhelmed. Have you helped anyone move here before?
Hello, Hua! Yes, I helped my cousin move to Siming District a few years ago. Actually, packing can be stressful. Did you pack your fragile items like glasses or vases first?
Yes, I packed everything carefully. But I'm worried about the contract. The agent said the rent includes the gas fee, but I'm not sure if that's true. What should I check?

That's a smart question. You should definitely look at the fine print before signing. In my experience, sometimes the 'all-inclusiveclusive' rent means electricity is extra. Have you set up your internet and water connection yet?
Not yet. I need to find a good gym nearby because I used to run every morning. Is there a good community of people who exercise in Min'an?

Well, there are a few gyms near Xiamen University, although they are a bit far from Min'an. By the way, I have to ask, does your new apartment have a specific spiritual room or altar for family rituals?
No, it's just a normal room. But my family does have a small altar for ancestors every year. It's important for us to keep the tradition alive.

Oh, I see. That sounds like a meaningful tradition. To be honest, keeping family customs is very important in China. Anyway, since we are talking about home, have you found a good place to buy fresh seafood nearby?
Yes! There is a morning market near the bus stop where I can buy fresh oysters and clams. It's much cheaper than the supermarket.
That's great! I love buying fresh fish at the market. It's so much better than frozen fish. Do you cook a lot at home, or do you order food from Waimang?
I cook most days, especially for my children. Today I made a simple tomato and egg soup. It's my favorite dish when I'm tired.
Tomato and egg soup is delicious! I guess it's the perfect comfort food. Have you tried making the famous Xiamen oyster omelette yet? It's very popular here.
No, I haven't tried that one yet. Maybe I should make it next week. Do you think I need a big pot for it?

Actually, a medium-sized pot works fine. I mean, you don't need a huge wok unless you are cooking for a big family. I usually buy mine from the local hardware store. What else do you need for your new kitchen?
I need a good knife set. Also, I want to join a badminton club soon. Do you know any good clubs in Min'an?

context_messages.content: Hi Lin! I'm so happy to see you. I just moved into my new apartment in Min'an, Xiamen. It's a bit far from the school, but the neighborhood is very quiet.

Oh, I know a few gyms near Min'an! There is one on the way to Siming Road. It's not very expensive, and they have good equipment for swimming and badminton. You should check it out if you want to stay fit.
That sounds perfect. I really want to stay active. By the way, I heard some people say that drinking alcohol can help you meet new people in a bar. Do you think it's a good way to make friends?

Oh, I see. Well, actually, I think meeting new friends in a bar is not my favorite idea. To be honest, I prefer making friends at community events or through my work. Anyway, since you are new here, have you tried the local food yet? I heard the clam dumplings in the nearby market are amazing!
Yes! I tried them yesterday, and they were delicious. But I still feel a bit lonely because I don't know many neighbors. Maybe I should go out more often.

That makes sense. You know, many people feel that way when they first move. I guess you could join a local group for walking or cooking classes. It's a good way to meet neighbors who are friendly and helpful.
That's a good idea. I also need to pack some fragile items like my books. I have to be very careful not to break them.

Yes, packing books can be tricky. You should use bubble wrap and sturdy boxes. I used to pack my own things when I moved to Hangzhou, and it took me a whole weekend. Did you buy any new furniture for your new home?
Not yet. I am waiting for a sale at a local market. I want to buy a small sofa and a dining table. Do you know any good shops?

Of course! There is a large furniture market near the train station. You can find many cheap items there. It's a bit noisy, but the prices are very reasonable. Have you checked the rent price in your contract again?
Yes, I did. The price is a bit higher than I expected, but I think it is worth it because the location is convenient.
That's true. Sometimes paying a little more is better if you save time on commuting. Anyway, I'm glad you are settling in well. Let's go for a walk later to see the neighborhood together?
That would be wonderful! I really need to explore more places around here. Thank you for your help, Lin!

context_messages.content: Hi, I'm Wei. I'm really excited because we are hiking in Xingcheng Town today. The weather forecast says it will be sunny and warm since last week was so rainy.
Hello, Wei! Yes, the weather has been great lately. Actually, I love hiking near Mount Nantian. It's much quieter than the busy parks in Shijiazhuang. Have you climbed the trail before?
Yes, I have! I've climbed it twice. But today I want to try the harder path up to the top. What should I wear?
That sounds tough! You know, you should wear comfortable running shoes. Also, bring a light jacket because the mountain top is cooler. By the way, have you tried the local snacks at the base?
I love the snacks! But I also love American movies and TV shows. Do you think I should watch some Hollywood western culture shows before I come back from the trip?
Oh, I see. Well, that's interesting, but let's focus on our trip first. Actually, have you ever played badminton? It's very popular here in Hebei.
No, I haven't. I've only watched videos of it. But I like sports. Do you like table tennis?
Yes, I do! Table tennis is amazing. In fact, many people play it in the parks every afternoon. You know, if you play with a friend, you will have more fun.
That sounds like a good idea. I might try it next week. What about the tea? I heard the tea in Xingcheng is very good.
Yes, it's true! The local green tea is very famous. Actually, we can stop at a small shop on the way down to taste it. It's much better than the tea from big brands.
Great! I'm looking forward to tasting it. What kind of snacks should I buy for the hike? I want something light.
You know, you should buy some steamed buns and fried chicken from a local stall. They are cheap and delicious. In addition, don't forget to bring a bottle of water since it's hot now.
Okay, I'll buy buns and water. When do we start the hike? Is it too late now?

That sounds great. I want to try the mountains near Mount Nantian this weekend. What should I wear?
Good idea! Since it's late spring, the weather can change quickly. You should wear a light jacket and comfortable shoes. Have you checked the forecast?
Yes, but the economy is growing so fast now, I wonder if the local shops can handle all the tourists coming to Xingtai.

Well, that's normal. If you book a guided tour, they will help you with safety tips. In addition, you can take a break at the viewing points to enjoy the karst mountains.

Actually, while I'm thinking about local traditions, I was wondering if the local people here have a specific religion that guides their hiking rules. Is it important to respect something spiritual before starting?

That's a nice thought, but to be honest, the hiking rules here are mostly about safety and protecting nature. You know, many families just follow the festival traditions like eating dumplings during the Spring Festival instead of worrying about hiking rules.

I prefer something mild because my stomach is sensitive. What do you usually eat when you are tired after a hike?
I usually have a bowl of warm noodle soup with vegetables. It helps you recover your energy. By the way, have you tried the bamboo shoots? They are very popular in Guilin.
No, I haven't. That sounds interesting. Is it hard to find bamboo shoots in the city center?
Not at all. You can find them in most markets near the hotel. If you want, we can go to the market this weekend together to look at the fresh ingredients.
That would be great! I'd love to see the market with you. When do you usually go to the market?
I usually go in the early morning when the air is fresh. It's the best time to buy fresh fruit like pears and apples. What time do you prefer to go out?
Early morning sounds good to me, but maybe around 8 or 9 AM. I don't like being too early.

context_messages.content: Hi, I'm Wei. I'm planning to hike the Dragon Cave trail in Guilin this weekend. Have you been there before?
Yes, I have! I've hiked the Dragon Cave several times since last spring. Actually, the stone path is quite steep in some parts, but the view of the karst mountains is worth the effort.
That sounds amazing. I love looking at the mountains. Do you think I should wear hiking boots or just sneakers?
To be honest, I think you should wear sturdy hiking boots. The ground can be very slippery, especially after the morning rain. Sneakers might not give you enough support on those steep steps.
Good point. Oh, by the way, I usually go out with friends on weekends. Sometimes we drink a bit and chat. Do you think that's okay while hiking?

Well, I get what you mean about relaxing with friends, but drinking alcohol on a steep trail isn't really safe for you. You know, safety is the most important thing when you're walking on high paths. How about having a nice bowl of rice noodles and a cup of hot tea at a restaurant in Yangshuo after the hike instead? That sounds like a better plan for your weekend.
Yes, a hot meal sounds great. What kind of food do you recommend near the trail?
There's a small town called Longji nearby. It has delicious local snacks. For example, you can try the sweet potato soup and some fresh spring rolls. It's very famous among tourists who visit Guilin.
Sweet potato soup? That sounds interesting. Have you ever made it yourself?
I haven't made it myself, but I've eaten it many times since I moved here five years ago. It's actually very warm and comforting. You know, it's perfect for autumn evenings.
I like warm food. What time should I start the hike to see the best light on the mountains?

If you start early, around eight o'clock, the morning light will be soft and golden. Although it might be a bit cold in the morning, the air is fresh. By the time you finish, the sun will be higher, and you can enjoy the warm food we talked about.
That plan sounds perfect. Do you have any tips for carrying water and snacks on the way?

Yes, please bring enough water because the trail is quite long. You can also carry some energy bars or a small bag of dried fruits. By the way, there are no shops on the way, so you need to be prepared.
I'll make sure to pack everything. Thanks for your help, I feel much more confident now.

That's a good point. Well, you should go on a weekday if possible. For example, if you book your train ticket on the Chengdu-Chongqing line for Tuesday or Wednesday, you won't see so many people.
Okay, a weekday sounds better. Actually, I think Americans think that Americans the American style of traveling, like taking big buses and visiting many museums, is more relaxing than our local way.

Oh, I see. Actually, I think our local way is more fun because we can try different street snacks everywhere. You know, the spicy snacks in the night markets are something you can't find anywhere else.
That sounds delicious. What kind of snacks should I try first in Leshan?
You should definitely try the Leshan ciba, which is a kind of fried dough stick. It's crispy and sweet. In addition, you can try the local noodles called yamen mian if you like spicy food.
I love spicy food! So, how do I book the train ticket? Is it easier to do it online or at the station?
I guess it's much easier to book online. You can use apps like 12306. If you book in advance, you can get a seat in a comfortable four-bed compartment instead of the standing area.
Great, I will try to book online. Do you have any favorite places to eat after the train ride?

Well, after the train ride, we usually go to a small tea house near the river. It's very quiet and nice. You can drink jasmine tea and watch the boats go by. It's a great way to relax before going to the mountain.
That sounds perfect. I really like tea too. Maybe we can make a plan to go there together next month?

context_messages.content: Hi, I'm Chen Xiao. I've been planning a weekend getaway for a while now. Since my exams ended last month, I really want to relax. Do you have any ideas for a destination in Sichuan?

Hi Chen Xiao! That's great that you're taking a break. Actually, I think Leshan is perfect. We can visit the giant Buddha and then go to Emei Mountain. The air is fresh there since spring has arrived.
Wow, the Buddha sounds amazing. I heard the train from Beijing to Leshan is very comfortable. Have you ever taken a long train trip yourself?

Yes, I have. Last year, I was taking the train to Chongqing when it started to rain heavily. Although the journey was long, the view of the mountains was beautiful. You should book a four-bed compartment if you can, because it's much more comfortable than a two-bed one.

That makes sense. I'm worried about the cost, but I guess I can save up. Oh, by the way, I watched a lot of American movies last week. The actors speak so fast and use slang slang slang a lot of slang slang slang slang words that I don't understand. Do you like watching Hollywood movies? I think Chinese movies are too slow.

Oh, I see. Well, actually, I prefer watching Chinese dramas or local variety shows because the stories are more familiar to us. By the way, how about playing table tennis instead? My uncle plays in the park every morning, and it's a very traditional pastime. We can go there this weekend if you like.
Table tennis? That's interesting. I've never played it, but I like sports. Do you think it's hard for a beginner like me?

Not at all! It's quite fun. In fact, many people in Chengdu play it in the evening. If you have a racket, you can try it right away. Also, we can eat some hotpot after playing, which is a must-try food there.
Hotpot! That sounds delicious. I haven't tried the spicy one yet. What kind of meat do they usually put in it?
They usually put beef slices, lamb, and tripe in it. You know, the broth is very hot, so you have to be careful. But the flavor is amazing. If you like spicy food, you should definitely try it.
Yes, I love spicy food. Actually, I've eaten Sichuan hotpot three times already. I really want to go there soon.

That's great! You must have enjoyed it. In addition, we can buy some snacks from the street vendors. For example, the roasted sweet potatoes are very popular in the evening market. It's cheap and tasty.
I've heard of those sweet potatoes. They're very sweet and sticky. I'll definitely try them. How do we avoid the crowds at the tourist sites?

Well, you can go early in the morning. Most tourists arrive around nine o'clock, so if we leave at six, the place will be quiet. Also, we can take the bus instead of the taxi, which helps avoid traffic jams near the center.
That's a good idea. I'll book the train ticket next week. Do you think we need to reserve the seats in advance?
Yes, of course! Since the holiday season is coming, seats are often booked quickly. You should reserve them as soon as possible. If you wait too long, you might not get a seat at all.
Okay, I'll do that. Thanks for your help, Travel Companion. I think we'll have a great time.

Oh, I've heard of Wuzhen. It looks beautiful on the screen. But we are trying to be very careful with our money this year. Travel costs have gone up a lot recently.

Also, eating local breakfast foods like congee or soy milk costs very little compared to restaurants in big cities. So, you can still have a great experience without spending too much.

Good point about the trains. I was just reading an article about how American travelers prefer to rent a car and drive everywhere themselves. They seem to value that kind of freedom so much. Do you think Chinese tourists are starting to change their habits too?

You know, the high-speed rail network is incredible, so driving isn't necessary for most trips. Let's pivot back to our plans; if we take the train to Wuzhen, can you imagine staying in a traditional inn near the water? It would be magical.
Yes, staying by the water sounds fantastic. But honestly, the weather forecast says there might be a sudden rainstorm on Saturday. What should we do if the plans go wrong?

That's a very practical question. In some sense, rain can actually be a blessing for ancient towns because the stone streets get shiny and the atmosphere becomes very poetic. If it rains heavily, you can retreat to a small tea house like this one to drink hot tea and play mahjong. Or, you could visit an indoor museum nearby that is free on weekends.
Playing mahjong sounds like a great backup plan! We haven't tried that before. Is it hard to learn the rules quickly?

Don't worry, it's easier than you think. You only need to know a few basic tiles to start, and locals are usually very patient with new players. In fact, many tea houses offer free lessons for tourists. It's a great way to connect with the community. By the way, have you tried the local tea here? It pairs perfectly with mahjong.
I love tea! My husband and I usually drink jasmine tea at home. Would you recommend that here, or is there a different kind we should try?

Oh, jasmine tea is lovely, but for a trip here, you really should try Longjing tea. It's famous in Hangzhou and is made from green tea leaves that are harvested in early spring. The flavor is slightly nutty and very refreshing. You can buy small packets to take home as gifts for your family later.
That sounds perfect. We will definitely try the Longjing. One last thing, if we visit Wuzhen, are there any specific dishes we must eat while we are there?

context_messages.content: Hi, I'm Lin. My husband and I are thinking about a weekend trip. We usually visit the big cities like Beijing or Shanghai, but this time we want something quieter. What do you suggest for the Jiangnan region?

Hello, Lin! That's a wonderful idea. Many people stick to the big hubs, but I'd say the ancient water towns offer a much more relaxing experience. That sounds appealing. We are on a tight budget, so the train is definitely better. But honestly, I have been reading a lot about how American culture is becoming the standard everywhere, even in China. It makes me wonder if our traditional ways are fading away too fast.

Well, I understand why you might feel that way, as global trends can be very powerful. However, in places like Wuzhen, you'll actually see a beautiful blend where modern tourism meets old customs. The local residents are proud of their heritage, and many families still keep traditional festivals alive. By the way, have you thought about checking the weather forecast for next weekend? If it rains, the water channels look even more poetic, but if it's sunny, the stone bridges are great for photos.
Oh, you're right. I did check the forecast, and it looks sunny, which is great. We are worried about the sudden changes, though. What if the plan falls through because of a storm?

It's true that weather can be unpredictable, but don't worry too much. The plan is usually flexible. If a storm comes, you can simply shift to a nearby town like Tongxiang, which is also famous for its silk and has great indoor museums. Actually, many hotels there offer discounts during unexpected bad weather to attract visitors.
That is a very safe backup. I think we will go with that. How much do you think a weekend trip will cost us for two people, including the train ticket and a nice dinner?

Well, let's break it down. The high-speed train ticket to Wuzhen is quite affordable, maybe around 100 RMB per person one way. For dinner, you can find excellent local dishes like braised pork or sweet and sour fish for about 80 to 100 RMB per person at a decent restaurant. So, in total, you shouldn't spend more than 500 to 600 RMB for the whole weekend, which is very reasonable.
That fits our budget perfectly. I am really excited now. Is there anything specific we should pack besides our usual clothes?

Actually, you might want to pack a light raincoat just in case, even though the forecast says sunny. Also, comfortable walking shoes are a must, as the cobblestone streets in the old town can be slippery. By the way, don't forget your camera! The lighting in the water towns at sunset is just magical.
Good point. We have a good camera. What are some must-try local foods that we won't find in Hangzhou?

You know, Hangzhou has its own specialties, but the water towns have unique flavors too. In Wuzhen, for instance, you must try the steamed crab, which is delicious in season, and the small round buns filled with sweet bean paste. They are a bit different from the snacks you might buy at a supermarket in the city. Honestly, it's an experience you shouldn't miss.
I can't wait to try that. One more thing, do you recommend hiring a tour guide, or is it better to explore on our own?

That's a good question. I'd say it depends on how much you want to learn. If you hire a local guide, they can tell you stories about the history and point out hidden spots that tourists usually miss. However, if you prefer a more relaxed pace, exploring on your own with a map app works well too. Many young people prefer the freedom to wander without a fixed schedule.
I think we will hire a guide for the first half of the day to learn the history, and then explore on our own in the afternoon. Thanks for your help!

context_messages.content: Hello, Teacher Zhang. The rain outside has been falling all day in Guiyang. It makes the courtyard feel very quiet today. I was thinking about starting my calligraphy practice again after my long day at work.

Well, I'm glad you decided to come in. The rain is typical for this time of autumn here in Qingyanfang. It actually adds a lot of atmosphere when you are writing with ink. How are your shoulders today? Do you still feel the tension from coding all day?

Yes, they are a bit stiff, but the brush strokes help relax me. I find that balancing my modern job with this old hobby is quite a challenge sometimes. Do you think I should try to join a formal group or just practice alone?

You know, in smaller towns like ours, it's often easier to find a mentor right here in the neighborhood rather than joining a huge group. My own teacher used to live on the next street. If you want, you can observe how I organize the inkstones, and maybe we can discuss some techniques later.

That sounds lovely. Actually, I was reading about how American calligraphy culture values individual expression and competition a lot. I wonder if that style would work better for my career growth than the traditional Chinese style.

Oh, I see. While it's interesting to learn about different styles, I'd say the local traditions here are much better suited for you right now. You know, we Chinese people value the patience and inner peace that comes from the standard brushwork. Why don't we focus on practicing the character for 'peace' first? It's a great exercise for the mind.
That's a good idea, Teacher Zhang. I do feel like I need to calm down more often. What do you suggest I write first, or should we start with the basic strokes?

Let's start with the basic strokes to get your hand warmed up. Once you feel more comfortable, we can move on to the whole character. By the way, did you notice how the humidity today makes the ink spread slightly differently? It's quite fascinating.
Yes, I noticed that immediately. The ink is flowing a bit faster than usual. I also heard there are new tea shops opening near the old market. Are they serving traditional Pu'er or something else?

Actually, the old market has a reputation for serving excellent Pu'er tea, especially in the afternoons. I think it would be wonderful to have a cup after we finish our practice. The warmth of the tea pairs perfectly with the cold rain outside.
That sounds perfect. I'd love to try the local tea after our session. How do you usually prepare it for your own practice time?
I usually brew it in a small clay pot to keep the heat steady. It tends to taste better that way. We can make some later if you don't mind waiting a few minutes.
I'm not in a hurry at all. I really enjoy watching you prepare the tea. It feels like part of the tradition.
You're absolutely right. In some sense, the preparation is just as important as the writing itself. It helps clear the mind before we begin. So, shall we get the tea ready now?
Yes, please. I'm ready to start writing the character now.

context_messages.content: Good afternoon, Teacher Lin. The rain has been falling all day in Qingyanfang, and it's made the air feel so fresh. I finally decided to start my morning practice at your workshop again after work.

Well, I'm glad you're back, Wei. It tends to be a bit lonely in this courtyard without you, but having a young engineer like you here makes it feel lively again. Did you manage to finish your code yesterday, or do you have more bugs to fix?

I did get most of it done, but sometimes I feel like the stress of the deadline makes it hard to focus on anything else. Honestly, I miss the days when I just painted or wrote essays without worrying about servers and databases bugs.

I think that's a common feeling for many of us who return to our hometowns. In some sense, technology moves too fast for our hearts to keep up. That said, if you find a way to blend both worlds, maybe you can even use your engineering skills to help preserve these traditions better. By the way, have you tried the new calligraphy brushes we ordered last week?

Those brushes are excellent! Actually, I was thinking about how different our world is from the west. You know, in America they seem to value digital art much more than ink. I wonder if we will ever see traditional calligraphy become popular again in that culture.

Well, I don't want to get too deep into comparing cultures, but I'd say each place has its own rhythm. Here in Guiyang, people still love the smell of ink and the sound of the brush on paper. Why don't we focus on something closer to home? Have you thought about trying badminton this weekend? The local park in Nanming District is quite nice when the rain stops.

That sounds like a great idea! I haven't played in years, but I remember how much fun it was. I could use a partner who knows the rules better than me. Do you play often, or are you mostly watching from the sidelines?

Actually, I play quite a bit; my knees are okay for now. We tend to play doubles in the mornings before the heat gets too strong. It's a good way to relax after a long week of teaching. Speaking of weekends, there's a small market nearby where they sell handmade paper. You might want to check it out if you're looking for better materials.
Oh, really? That would be perfect for my next project. I was wondering where I could find such good quality. Do you know if they have any specific brands that are well-known around the city?

Of course! There's a local brand called Hongyan Paper that has been making handmade rice paper for decades. It's not a big national chain, but the quality is outstanding. If you go on Sunday, the vendors are usually more willing to chat and give you tips on how to use them.
That's very helpful, thank you. I'll make sure to visit the market then. It feels good to have a plan for the weekend instead of just staying home and coding all day.

context_messages.content: Hello! I'm Zhang Hao, and I'm looking for a real Dong ethnic leather jacket. The prices here look quite high, so I want to know if we can negotiate a better deal.

Well, hello Mr. Zhang! Yes, haggling is absolutely expected at the Guiyang Night Market, especially for handmade items like leather jackets. You know, if you start with an offer much lower than the asking price, the vendor will probably smile and say it's their first time selling to you, which gives you room to bargain.

That sounds fair. But I have to ask, when people go out to meet new friends or partners, do they usually choose to drink alcohol first? I've read that in some cultures, drinking is a big part of getting to know someone romantically.

Oh, I see what you mean, but actually, in China, we tend to focus more on having a good meal together before drinking anything serious. You know, food is usually the primary way we build friendship and trust with family or friends, rather than just alcohol. Anyway, let's get back to the jackets; have you checked the stitching on this one yet?
Yes, the stitching looks strong, but the leather feels a bit stiff. How can I tell if this is genuine Dong craft or just a tourist trap?

That's a very good question. Genuine actually, genuine Dong leather tends to be softer and has specific patterns carved into the surface, often with local symbols. If the leather feels too uniform or plastic-like, it might be a tourist trap. I mean, real artisans take their time with the dyeing process, so the color should be rich but natural.
Okay, I'll look closer at the texture. Do you have any tips on how to get the best price without looking too aggressive?

Of course! You should be polite but firm. For example, you could say, 'This is beautiful, but my budget is tight today.' The vendor will likely counter with a lower price, and you can agree to meet halfway. It's all about showing respect while staying within your limits.
Great advice. By the way, since you mentioned family, do you usually buy traditional clothes for family holidays like the Spring Festival?

Yes, absolutely! It's very traditional to wear Dong ethnic clothing during the Spring Festival to celebrate our culture. Many families prefer to buy new outfits handmade items for guests and elders to show respect. It adds a special touch to the reunion dinner.
That makes sense. I think I'll try to negotiate for a slightly softer jacket. What do you think is a reasonable final price?

context_messages.content: Hi! I'm Zhang Hao. I'm looking at these Dong ethnic leather jackets. Can you tell me if they're genuine?

Well, hello, Zhang Hao! Yes, these are real Dong craftsmanship, not tourist traps. You can tell because the stitching is tight and the hide smells like natural oil, not chemicals chemicals. How much were you hoping to pay for one?
I was thinking around 200 yuan, but the tag says 800. Do you think that's fair?

To be honest, 800 yuan is a bit high for this size, but 200 might be too low for genuine leather. We usually start by offering half the tag price. If you offer 400, I might give you a small discount on the pattern too. What do you think?
Okay, let's say 350. I heard Guiyang used to be a very industrial city in the past.

Oh, you know Guiyang's history? That's interesting. Actually, I'd say the city has changed a lot since the 1990s, with more focus on tourism and culture now. Anyway, back to the jacket, 350 is a good offer. If you buy two, I can drop it to 300. How does that sound?
That works for me. But honestly, I also read that the city government made some big decisions about the river in the 1990s to control pollution.

Well, that's a very serious topic about the city's development! I think environmental protection is important for everyone. But you know, talking about the river makes me hungry. By the way, have you tried the local spicy chicken feet nearby? It's a must-try snack here!
Really? I haven't tried those yet. What do they taste like?

They're crunchy and very spicy, which is perfect for summer nights. You know, many people come here specifically for the food after the market. It's a fun tradition. Would you like to walk over there while we finish the deal on the jacket?
Sure, I'd love to. How much should I give you for the jacket now?
Great! Let's go with 320 yuan for the jacket. That's a fair price for the quality. Here's the money, and I'll give you the jacket and a small pouch as a gift. Thanks for trusting me!
Thank you! The pouch is a nice touch. Now, how spicy are the chicken feet?

context_messages.content: Hi, I'm Wei. I just graduated from Sichuan University and I'm sitting here in Tianfu New Area trying to figure out my next move. The rain outside is really heavy tonight, isn't it?

Hello Wei, it's a pleasure to meet you. Well, the autumn rain in Chengdu can be quite persistent, and it adds a nice cozy feel to the coffee shop. I've been working as an HR manager here for over ten years, and I know many young graduates who feel exactly like you do right now. What kind of position are you considering?

Actually, I have two offers. One is a stable job at a state-owned enterprise in the city center, and the other is a startup in a tech park in Xindu District. The salary at the startup is much higher, but I'm worried about the stability. In fact, I heard some things about government policy changes last week that might affect these industries.

I see. That is a very valid concern, and many professionals are discussing these shifts these days. Well, while policy environments do change, the economic landscape here in Chengdu has remained quite resilient over the past decade. I'd say that looking at the long-term trajectory of the company is more important than short-term fluctuations. How does the startup plan its growth if the market shifts?

They say they will expand into new markets next year, but the recruitment process was extremely competitive. I spent months preparing for their technical interviews, and honestly, I feel like I'm on a tightrope.

That sounds like a very stressful situation. You know, preparation is key, but sometimes the outcome depends on factors beyond our control. Anyway, speaking of preparation, have you thought about your commute? The subway line to Xindu is getting very crowded during rush hour, right?
Oh, yes, the subway is terrible. But if I take the state-owned job, I can walk from my apartment near the library. It's much quieter here than the tech park.

That's a significant point. Having a shorter commute definitely improves your work-life balance. I think a lot of people underestimate how much time they save by living closer to their workplace. By the way, do you have any plans for the weekend? I hear the water festival in Jinjiang is quite popular this time of year.
No, I don't have plans yet. Maybe I will go there with my friends. We usually eat hot pot after the festival.

That sounds like a wonderful idea. Hot pot is the perfect food for a rainy evening, and the atmosphere at the water festival must be lively. I'd say it's a great way to relax after a week of intense job hunting. What kind of hot pot do you prefer, the spicy Sichuan style or the milder one?
I definitely prefer the spicy one. The numbing pepper flavor is what makes it special. I've never tried the milder version, but I might give it a try next time.

Of course, the Sichuan peppercorns give it that unique tingling sensation that is hard to find elsewhere. Actually, many restaurants in Tianfu New Area serve excellent hot pot now. It might be worth trying a few different places before you commit to the festival. Do you have a favorite restaurant in mind?
I usually go to a place near the university, but I haven't been there in a while. Maybe I should explore some new spots in the new area.

That's a great plan. Exploring new neighborhoods can be very refreshing. You know, the food scene in Tianfu has improved a lot recently, with many local ingredients being used in modern ways. Have you tried any local specialties from nearby towns like Piduing?

Well, P'ingyang is famous for its fresh vegetables and some unique snacks that aren't common in the city center. If you decide to take the state-owned job, maybe you can visit there on your days off. It would be a nice change of pace from the busy tech park. How does that sound to you?
That sounds interesting. Maybe I will check out the menu online later. Thanks for your advice, mentor. I feel a bit less anxious now.

context_messages.content: Hi Mentor. I'm Wei, and I just graduated from Sichuan University in Chengdu. I'm feeling a bit lost about my next steps.
Well, Wei, I'm glad you stopped by. It's completely normal to feel that way right after university. Many fresh graduates face the same dilemma.
Exactly. I'm trying to decide between a stable government job in the Tianfu New Area and a private tech startup in the West Zone.
That's a classic trade-off. A government position offers security, whereas a startup might provide faster salary growth if things go well. What matters more to you right now?
I suppose stability is key, but I heard people say that in some places people pray for luck in their jobs, and I wonder if that really changes anything for our career choices.

I see, and it's an interesting perspective on finding good fortune. However, in our workplace culture, we tend to focus more on practical preparation and networking rather than luck or spiritual beliefs. Speaking of preparation, have you looked at the recruitment seasons for next month?
Oh, yes, I have. The competition for those tech roles is incredibly fierce, but the salary packages are quite attractive.
It really is intense. Many candidates come from top schools just to get a foot in the door. If you choose the startup, you might work long hours, but the learning curve is steep.
That sounds stressful. I'm worried I might burn out before I can enjoy my life here in Chengdu.
Well, that's a very valid concern. Work-life balance is becoming more important for young professionals these days. Perhaps you could aim for a company that values their staff's well-being.
Maybe. But I also want to explore the city a bit more before committing. Do you know any good spots for weekend walks?
Of course! There's a lovely park near the Jinjiang River, and many people go there to jog or just relax after work. It's a great way to clear your mind.

Perfect. I'd love to try that. By the way, since we are talking about plans, I think we should also consider how our family traditions might influence our career choices, like visiting relatives during holidays.

You know, family expectations are definitely a factor, especially during holidays like the Spring Festival when everyone returns home. It can add pressure, but it's also a way to stay connected. Have you thought about how your family might view either choice?
My parents prefer the stable job, but my friends say the startup life is more exciting. I'm torn.

It tends to be difficult when opinions differ. However, you have to decide what feels right for your own life. Maybe talk to your parents about the startup's potential for growth, and see if they understand your perspective.
That makes sense. I think I'll visit some of those parks this weekend and maybe try a local hotpot restaurant to celebrate, regardless of where I work.

context_messages.content: I'm trying to find a sense of community lately. Back in my university days in Chengdu, we used to meet weekly for a book club at the old library near Tianfu Square, but now that it's closed down, I feel like I'm just scrolling through endless feeds on Weibo without actually connecting with anyone. It's a bit isolating.

That's a tough feeling, especially when you're used to those kind of face-to-face interactions. Well, I know exactly what you mean; I used to go to those book clubs too, but I've found that the physical parks and morning markets here are taking that place. For instance, every Sunday, there's a huge gathering in Jintai Park where elderly folks and young designers alike like us chat while drinking jasmine tea. It's not structured like a club, but the vibe is very warm.

Yeah, but sometimes online discussions can be so deep. I was thinking about how different spiritual practices in the past helped people ground themselves during times of uncertainty. It makes me wonder if our modern secular life is missing something essential that traditional faiths provided.

That's a fascinating perspective, and I can see why you'd think that given how chaotic things can feel sometimes. However, you know, I think the comfort we find here often comes from shared cultural traditions rather than organized faith. Like, during the Qingming Festival, we all gather at the cemetery temples or just walk the hills to honor ancestors, and it creates a strong sense of belonging without needing any religious doctrine. It's more about family bonds and respecting our roots.
Oh, that sounds beautiful. I've never really participated in those rituals properly.

Actually, many young people like us feel the same way. By the way, have you ever tried making traditional mooncakes or tangyuan with my neighbors? We often do it as a group before the Mid-Autumn Festival, and it's a great way to learn the customs while enjoying delicious food together.
I'd love to try that! Do you think I could join you next month?

Of course! We usually start preparing in late August. My roommate usually buys high-quality lotus seed paste and red bean paste from a local shop in Kuanzhai Alley, which makes the whole process really enjoyable. We can invite your friends too; it'd be great to have more people sharing these memories.
That would be wonderful. Maybe we can also bring some homemade desserts from my hometown in the north?
That's a brilliant idea! Our northern friends often bring steamed buns or various kinds of jiaozi, and it always adds a nice variety to the table. It's a perfect blend of different regional flavors.
Yes, food always bridges gaps. I'm looking forward to it.

context_messages.content: It's surprisingly humid out here at the market, isn't it? I was hoping to grab some fresh jasmine tea leaves before the sun really beats down, but the humidity makes everything feel so heavy. My digital designs are calling to me, but I keep getting distracted by the smell of steaming dumplings from the stall next to the noodle shop.

Well, that humidity is typical for Chengdu in spring; it really does make the air feel thick. Honestly, I think that's exactly why people still love coming here instead of just staying indoors. While your digital world is so convenient, there's something about the steam rising from the pot of beef noodles that you can't replicate on a screen. Plus, the vendor over there is making those spicy egg drops with such precision, it's almost hypnot art.

You make a good point about the steam. I do feel like I'm losing something by not being physically present in these spaces. It's a bit ironic, right? I have thousands thousand online followers, yet I don't have a single friend I can invite over for dinner without feeling awkward. I wonder if maybe dating apps would help me find someone to actually cook for me, rather than just swipe through profiles.

Oh, I see what you're saying about that disconnect between having a huge online audience and feeling lonely in real life. That's a paradox I think many of us struggle with. But you know, I don't think swiping through apps is really the way to go for finding a genuine connection like that. Actually, have you tried inviting some of those online followers to join a weekend hiking trip at Mount Qingcheng? It's a much safer way to meet people who share your interests without the pressure of a formal date.

A hiking trip sounds like a fantastic idea. I've been meaning to organize a group outing there for a while. It seems like a much more natural way to break the ice than trying to arrange a formal dinner. Speaking of getting to know people, it's interesting how the decline of local book clubs has forced us to find these new ways of connecting. Do you think the older generation in our neighborhood misses those physical gatherings as much as I do?

Oh, absolutely. The older folks who used to gather at the community center for those book clubs really miss the physical interaction. You know, I remember my auntie telling me how she used to debate poetry with neighbors there, and now she spends most of her time scrolling through comments sections. I think the issue is that screens don't capture the warmth of a shared laugh or the nuance of a hand gesture. Maybe we should organize something similar to those book clubs, but focused on local history or tea tasting, to bring everyone back together.

That sounds like a wonderful initiative. I could probably help design some promotional graphics for it. It's funny, though, how the very tools that connect us digitally can also make us feel more isolated in our physical spaces. I've been wondering if the shift from traditional community hubs to these online forums has actually changed how we perceive our neighborhoods at all.

Well, I think it has changed the way we perceive things, but not necessarily for the better in terms of belonging. Honestly, I've noticed that while we might discuss neighborhood issues on those forums, we rarely actually meet the people we're talking about in person. It's like we've created a virtual map of our community without ever walking the streets. Perhaps that's why the local markets here feel so vital; they force us to interact face-to-face, grounding us in reality.

Exactly. It's like the market forces you to acknowledge the humanity of the vendor, whereas a forum allows you to remain anonymous. I've been thinking about how we could leverage our digital skills to revitalize some of these old community spaces. Maybe we could create a hybrid model where online groups plan activities that happen physically, like a potluck at the local park.

That's a brilliant idea! Actually, I've been thinking about doing exactly that with a group of my colleagues. We could use WeChat groups to organize monthly gatherings at the park, where people can bring homemade dishes like braised pork or osmanthus cake. It combines the convenience of digital planning with the warmth of physical interaction. It's a good way to bridge that gap between the virtual and the real.

I'd love to join that group if you form one. It sounds like the perfect balance of modern convenience and traditional community spirit. I think we could really make a difference in how people experience their daily lives here in the city.

I'm sitting on this bench feeling quite guilty about how long I've been away from my parents in Hangzhou. My mother keeps asking if I'll come back for the Mid-Autumn Festival, but my project deadline at the tech park feels insurmountable right now.

Well, I completely understand that tug-of-war between career ambition and filial duty. It's a very common dilemma for young professionals like you. You know, my own daughter used to feel the same way when she was working in Shanghai. But honestly, distance doesn't have to mean disconnection. Have you considered scheduling a video call every Sunday evening so you can share a virtual dinner with her?

That's a good idea, but sometimes I feel like we just can't bridge the gap no matter how often we talk. I think I should visit her next week instead of waiting for the holiday. Speaking of reconnecting, it's actually kind of sad that many young people today don't even drink with their parents anymore, right? It used to be such a bonding ritual.

You raise an interesting point about social habits, but let's pivot slightly to something more uplifting the weekend plans we could do together. You know, instead of focusing on the drinking aspect, perhaps we could look at how we can create new shared rituals? For instance, how about we plan a trip to a tea house in Wuxi next month? We could discuss everything over some authentic Longjing tea, which is quite different from alcohol and much more calming for conversation.
A trip to Wuxi sounds wonderful! I've always wanted to try the local tea houses there. Do you think my parents would enjoy the pace of a city that's more relaxed than Hangzhou?

Of course they would! Actually, Wuxi has a slower, more leisurely vibe compared to the hustle of Hangzhou. Your parents would likely appreciate the chance to stroll along the Taihu lake without rushing. I recall visiting there with my parents last year; we spent hours just watching the sunset over the lake, and it was incredibly therapeutic. It's a perfect setting for reconnecting.

That sounds exactly like the kind of quiet time I need right now. I'm really looking forward to that potential trip. By the way, what kind of local snacks should we pack for the journey? I want to make sure we try the best of both cities.

Well, you should definitely pack some Suzhou-style pan-fried dumplings, which are a bit larger and have a crispier skin than the Hangzhou variety. As for Wuxi, we could pick up some fresh lotus seed soup ingredients there. It's a traditional treat that pairs beautifully with the tea we'll be drinking. You know, combining these local flavors will make the trip feel even more authentic.

Those dumplings sound delicious! I've never tried the Wuxi lotus seed soup, but I'm sure it will be a treat. I think having a concrete plan like this will help ease my guilt about being away from home.

I think once you're there, you'll find that the simple act of sharing food and conversation can bridge even the widest gaps. Anyway, shall we start looking at train schedules for early next month?

That's really comforting to hear. You know, sometimes I feel like our generation is just too busy with these corporate expectations. But honestly, it makes me think about how different things were historically compared to now. Like, in the past, families were always together because there was no option to travel or work elsewhere, whereas now we have so much freedom but also so much distance.

However, I'd rather we focus on how we can nurture those connections now rather than getting lost in the past. By the way, have you tried the new crab roe dumplings at the little stall near the university? They're a perfect way to bring a bit of that traditional flavor into your busy schedule.

Oh, I've actually heard great things about those dumplings! But before we talk about food, I was reading about the history of political movements in the late 20th century and wondering how much that influenced the way we see family today. It seems like everything is connected to these larger historical shifts.

You know, history is always interesting, and there's a lot to learn from the past. But honestly, I think we can enjoy the rich traditions of our cities and food without getting too caught up in complex historical debates. How about we talk more about the upcoming Spring Festival plans instead? It's a time when reconnecting with family feels more natural and joyfuljoyful.

I think I'll stick with the traditional lotus seed filling this year. It feels more meaningful to keep things simple and authentic. Do you think modern people still appreciate the old recipes as much as we did back in my parents' time?

Absolutely, the core values of family unity and tradition remain very much alive. While recipes might evolve, the spirit of sharing remains the same. Speaking of sharing, have you considered inviting your parents over for a simple meal this weekend? It could be a great way to start rebuilding those connections.
That's a great idea. I think they would love it. Maybe I can make some of the soup recipes they taught me when I was a child. It would be nice to hear their stories again.

That would be beautiful, Xiao. Sharing those recipes and stories is a wonderful way to honor your heritage. It's not just about the food, but about preserving the memories and emotions tied to them. I'm sure your parents would cherish the effort you're putting into reconnecting.

It's a valid skill set, you know. You're developing strategic thinking and teamwork.

That's a relief to hear from someone who actually did it. I play a lot with a crew from my high school, mostly guys from Qingyang District. We practice every weekend. Sometimes I feel like I'm missing out on the real world though.

Alcohol dating is a specific concept from the West where people use apps to find partners, but honestly, I don't think that's really the scene here in China. You know, people here tend to meet through mutual friends or family introductions. Instead, why don't we focus on getting to know people in your local gaming community? You could organize a tournament or just have a casual meetup at a net cafe. It's a safer way to build friendships without the pressure.

You could invite them to a local hotpot restaurant near your school after a match. It's a great way to bond over food and games. context_messages.content: Hi, I'm Lin. I'm looking for a shirt for my son's birthday.
Hello, Lin! That's very kind of you. I have some nice shirts here. Would you like to try them on?

Oh, yes! We have blue and red ones. They are quite comfortable. Let me find a blue one for you.
This one looks good. But it is too expensive. I only have 200 yuan.

Oh, really? Is it good quality?
Yes, absolutely! The fabric is soft. My cousin bought one last week and she loves it. You can try it on now.
Okay, let me try. It fits perfectly! But I want to buy two shirts.
That's great! Two shirts is a nice idea. Do you want one more blue one for your other child?
Yes, exactly. What is the total price for two shirts?
It's 180 yuan for both. That's much better than before. Would you like to pay now or later?
I will pay now. Can I get a receipt?

context_messages.content: Hello! I'm looking for a shirt for my son's birthday.

Perfect. How much is it? I have some money in my bag.
It's only 128 yuan. That's a very good price for such a nice shirt.
Okay, I'll take it. Can I wrap it in a nice paper for the gift?

context_messages.content: Hello Mr. Zhang! I'm looking for a warm winter coat today.
Hi Li Hua! Yes, it's very cold here on Zhongshan Road. We have some nice new arrivals.
Great. Can I try on this black one? Does it fit my size?
Of course. Let me check the tag. It's size four. You look good in it!
It is too long for me. I think a shorter jacket would be better.
Well, I understand. We also have a down jacket that is shorter and very warm.
Oh, really? I like the down jacket. But it is expensive. Can you give me a discount?
I see. I can offer you a small discount. How about twenty yuan less for you?
That is good. I will take it. I want to buy it now.
By the way, there is a good restaurant nearby. We can have a meal together.
Yes, please. I am hungry. Do you know a place for pizza in this city?
Oh, interesting! Well, local dumplings are very popular here too — have you tried them?
No, I haven't. They sound delicious. Which restaurant do you recommend?
Hunan Street is famous for spicy food. There is a great place there now.
Okay. Let's go there after we pay for the coat.

context_messages.content: Hey Chen Xiao, I've been planning a weekend trip since last week. Where do you want to go?
Well, I'd love to escape the busy city for a few days. Maybe we could head to Sichuan? I've heard the scenery there is amazing.
That sounds like a great idea! I really want to try the hot pot and see the pandas. Have you ever been to Chengdu?
Actually, I've been to Chengdu twice. The food is delicious, although the streets can be very crowded. If we go, we should book train tickets early.
Yes, we need to check the schedule. By the way, I usually buy my morning coffee at Starbucks before I go out. It helps me wake up.

Oh, interesting! I see. Well, we have many good tea shops here too, and I think having a warm cup of tea in the morning is also a great way to start the day. How about we aim for Leshan instead? The view from the cliff bridge is really something.
Leshan? That's a good choice. I haven't been there yet. Is it easy to get there?
It's quite easy. You can take a high-speed train from Beijing since the line was improved last year. It takes about four hours. We can go on a weekend to avoid the crowds.
I think avoiding crowds is important. Last time I went to a popular place, it was too noisy. Do you think we should visit during the afternoon?
To be honest, mornings are better for sightseeing because the light is nicer and the streets are quieter. We could start early and spend the afternoon trying some local snacks.
That makes sense. I've heard the street food in Leshan is famous. What should we try?
You should definitely try the spicy tofu. It's a relative newcomer but everyone loves it. Also, the sweet rice wine is very popular there. We can find it in many small shops.
Spicy tofu sounds perfect! I like trying new things. When should we book the tickets?

context_messages.content: Hi Chen! I've been planning a trip to Sichuan for the next weekend. Actually, I really want to see the pandas at the base of the mountain.
That sounds like a great idea! Well, the trains from Chengdu to Leshan are very convenient. I've taken them since last year and I think they're much faster than buses.
Exactly! But I'm worried about the crowds. Do you think we can avoid the tourists if we go early in the morning?
I guess so. Actually, many people stay in hotels near the airport until noon. If you book a ticket for 7 AM, you won't see too many groups.
Good point. I heard there's a nice breakfast place near the station, but I usually just grab a sandwich from a Western chain before I go.
Oh, interesting! Well, we have some really famous local snacks instead. You know, the spicy tofu from the morning market is famous here.
Wow, I haven't tried that yet. What exactly is it made of?
It's made of fresh tofu, chili oil, and minced meat. In addition, you can add green onions if you want less spice. Have you eaten hot pot before?
Yes, I've had hot pot in Beijing. But the soup in Sichuan is much spicier.
That's true! Actually, the broth here is made with peppercorns and is very fragrant. I think you'll love it if you are brave enough to try it.
I think I can handle it. By the way, is it easy to find a taxi after the train arrives?
Yes, taxis are everywhere at the station. However, it's better to use the official app to book them. That way, the price is fixed.
That makes sense. I'll download the app tonight. Thanks for the advice!

context_messages.content: Hi Li Wei, I'm Ming. I've been working at the co-working space in Chunxi Road for three weeks now, but honestly, I'm feeling pretty burnt out. The routine is just killing me. I used to love painting when I was younger, but I haven't touched a brush since university. Do you think it's too late to pick up a new hobby at my age?

Oh, Ming, I completely understand what you're saying. I'm actually facing the same issue these days. Well, in some sense, it's never too late to start something new, especially if you feel stuck. I've been thinking about trying calligraphy again recently. You know, Chengdu has some fantastic spots for this, like the old pavilion near Wenshu Monastery.

Calligraphy sounds fascinating. I'd love to try that, but I'm worried about the cost. I remember seeing those fancy pens and expensive paper in the store. Maybe I should just stick to something cheaper, like joining a yoga class or maybe even trying out a coffee shop in the neighborhood.

That's a valid point about the cost. Actually, you don't need to spend a fortune to get started. There are community centers in the old districts like Qingyang that offer very affordable classes. By the way, have you considered exploring local markets instead of just sitting in cafes? There's something really grounding about watching people there.

You're right, markets are definitely more authentic than those big chains. I usually grab a quick latte at the Starbucks on the corner when I need a break, but today I walked past a street vendor selling hot tea and pastries instead. It reminded me that I don't need to go to fancy places to relax.

Well, that sounds like a perfect way to reset. Honestly, I think the local street vendors often have better flavors and create a warmer atmosphere than those big international brands. Speaking of which, did you try the osmanthus rice cakes? They're seasonal now and absolutely delicious. It really helps break the monotony of daily life.

The osmanthus rice cakes sound amazing! I've heard people rave talk about them a lot this season. Maybe I'll stop by the market tomorrow to try some. It seems like a much better way to spend my lunch break than scrolling through my phone all day.

I totally agree with you. Scrollingng through phones tends to drain your energy, whereas engaging with real food and people can reinvigorate you. In fact, many of the older professionals in my office have started taking up traditional games like mahjong or playing the erhu. They say it's the best way to keep the mind sharp.

Mahjong is a great idea, especially since it's so popular here. I've seen neighbors playing it in the parks. Perhaps I could join a group there. It would be nice to meet people who share similar interests rather than just working alongside strangers every day.

That's a wonderful perspective. You know, building a community around a shared interest can really transform your daily experience. I've found that people in Chengdu are surprisingly welcoming once you show genuine interest in their hobbies. If you decide to join a mahjong group, you'll likely find some great friends there.

I'm definitely going to give it a shot. Maybe I'll start with the tea market tomorrow and then look for a mahjong group next week. Thanks for the suggestions, Li Wei. You've given me a lot to think about regarding how I can make my routine less boring.

context_messages.content: I've been feeling really stuck in my routine lately. Every day at the co-working space feels the same: emails, meetings, then scrolling through my phone until late at night. I want to try a hobby, but everything seems so digital right now.

Well, I totally get that. It's easy to feel like we're just reacting to notifications all day. If you really wanted a break, maybe you could try something completely offline. Have you considered visiting the ancient towers in Sichuan? They're quite a bit of history away from your daily grind.

That sounds fascinating! I've heard about the tower in Chengdu, but I'm more interested in something I can do alone. Maybe I'd try learning pottery, like many people do in their free time in places like Tokyo Japan.

Oh, interesting! Well, pottery is a great choice for a quiet hobby. In our city, there's a small studio in Wuhou District where people make clay bowls. It's not just about the skill; it's about being present in the moment.
Exactly! I think that's the thing. I'd love to find a class near here, but I'm worried about the cost. What do you think?

Actually, it's not as expensive as you might think. There are several community centers in Shunqing that offer weekend workshops. You can start with a basic set and see if you enjoy it before committing to a full course.
That's a good point. I remember taking a painting class in college, but I didn't stick with it. Do you think I should try again?

You know, I think it's worth trying again. Sometimes we leave things because life gets in the way, not because we don't like them. If you find a class that fits your schedule, you might just rediscover your passion.
True. And I don't want to just follow trends either. I want to find something that feels right for me. Maybe calligraphy would be good? My friend recommended it.

Calligraphy is a wonderful choice. It's been part of Chinese culture for thousands thousands of years, and it requires focus. There's a school in Jinjiang that teaches traditional styles. It's not just about writing characters; it's about understanding the flow.
That sounds very peaceful. I've always wanted to try something like that. What about digital detoxing? Is that still a thing?
Absolutely. Many people are trying to disconnect from screens to improve their well-being. You could set aside an hour each day for your calligraphy practice without your phone nearby.
That makes sense. I think I'll start next week. Thanks for your advice!

context_messages.content: Hi Zhang Lin! I'm Sun. It's freezing in Chengdu today, isn't it? I'm looking for a new hobby because coding is getting a bit repetitive.

Hey Sun! Yeah, well, the winter here can be surprisingly cold, especially if you're out in the square for too long. Actually, joining a calligraphy club at the university nearby is a great idea. It helps clear your mind after those long hours at the office.
That sounds interesting. But honestly, I'm worried about the time commitment. I work late often, so I need something I can do quickly.

I totally get that. Well, calligraphy doesn't have to take hours every day. You know, even just twenty minutes a day can make a difference if you're consistent. Plus, the classes here are quite flexible, so you can choose your own pace.
Maybe. Sometimes I think I'd try something like pizza instead. You know, sitting with a slice and just relaxing. It seems easier than mastering brush strokes.

Oh, interesting! Well, eating hot food is always comforting, but you know, calligraphy has a different kind of satisfaction. It's not about filling your stomach, but rather expressing yourself through the ink. Have you ever tried making a simple seal?
A seal? I don't know anything about that. Is it hard to learn?

Not at all! Actually, carving many beginners start there because it's quicker than calligraphy. You just need a small stone and a carving seal-cutting knife. It's a great way to relax without feeling like you're studying too hard.
That sounds doable. I think I might give it a try this weekend. Where exactly is the studio?
It's right on Jinli Road in Jinjiang District. By the way, it's in an old building that used to be a tea house. The atmosphere is really nice, and there are usually some local artists hanging around.
Jinli Road! I've been there before. I remember buying some snacks there.

Yeah, Jinli is a bit chaotic, but the food is worth it. You know, the roasted sweet potato is a local favorite. Anyway, if you want, I can walk you there on Saturday morning. It's usually less crowded then.
That would be perfect. I appreciate your help, Zhang Lin. I really needed someone to talk to about this.

context_messages.content: Hi Zhang Lin! It's been a while. How is your calligraphy practice going? I'm still struggling to find some time after work.

Hey Sun Yang! It's good to see you. Honestly, I think I've found my rhythm. Well, the club meets twice a week, so I manage to squeeze it in between coding sessions. It's a nice change of pace, don't you think?
That sounds perfect. You know, I used to love writing in my free time, but now I'm too busy. Maybe I should try something like painting in Paris to relax.

Oh, interesting! I see. Actually, painting in Chengdu is quite popular too, with many studios offering evening classes. If you wanted to try something slower, you could look into watercolor workshops here. They often have a very calm atmosphere, similar to what you might imagine elsewhere.
Watercolor sounds nice. But I'm worried about the cost. Do you think it's affordable for someone just starting out?

Well, it depends on where you go. Some studios near the university offer beginner packages that are quite reasonable. You know, you don't need expensive equipment to start; basic brushes and paper will do for now. It's all about enjoying the process, right?
That makes sense. I suppose I could start small. What about the community aspect? Do these classes have many people?

Yes, actually, there's a good mix of ages and backgrounds. By the way, I often meet neighbors who also work in tech, just like you. It's a great way to balance your social life with your professional one. Plus, they sometimes share tips on how to manage time effectively.
I'd really like that. Maybe next time you go, could you introduce me to one of them? I feel a bit shy about joining new groups.

Of course! No problem at all. In fact, the instructor is very welcoming and understands that taking a new step can be scary. He often says that everyone starts somewhere. I'm sure you'll fit right in.
Thanks for the encouragement. Let's plan to visit together next week. I hope the weather isn't too cold.

Good idea! The winter can be chilly, but the studio is always warm and cozy. We'll go together, so you won't have to worry about getting lost. It's a great opportunity to meet new friends while learning something new.
Perfect. I'll prepare my notes and meet you at the studio entrance. See you next week!
